I think for many millenials (like myself) we were raised in a culture of "buying shit we don't need with money we don't have". I personally felt, and was viewed as successful due to the items I "owned" despite having loans for everything.

In 2006 I overpaid for a house I could barely afford at the time with no money down and it was handyman special. In 2015, 9 years of marriage and 2 kids later I sold the house for 10k less than I paid for it, put 20k into plus hundreds of hours of labor, to show up to a closing and PAY 5k out of pocket to sell my house.

This experience has made me feel quite stupid. How could I have been so stupid? I had no money but the bank said "No problem sign here!" They said the same for multiple car loans, appliances, you name it I could finance it.

(Kids need help will continue after I am done being a dad for the day)

Edit: Ok back. So in early 2015 I sold my house, left the state of CT with my family to start a new life in Florida. For the first time in my life I was near debt free except for an auto loan.

The financial reset for me allowed me to look at things from a different perspective and make better choices. I started to define what I "needed" vs "wanted". Wants are cash only. Needs? Define need? What will happen if I don't have this item or service?

The end result of this thought process is a lack of loans and the ability to save. I went from a family of 4 with an income of 105k to an income of 85k yet I feel like I have significantly more money. (Back when I'm done being a dad, again)

Edit: Ok back. So more money. More money comes from less consuming. I want to buy a house again and I want to do it with a healthy down payment, I also want to pay it off early if possible. I am much more particular about financing terms. I also analyze everything and try to be honest with myself.

Here is an example: We had 2 years left on our auto loan for our 2008 Mercury Mountaineer. I personally maintained it and it was in very good shape. We no longer needed an SUV and my wife would prefer a car. I'm not willing to spend more than 10% of my gross income on a car so that put my price range at no more than 8.5k. I looked and compared for months. I am perfectly capable of making a 450 dollar a month car payment but that is ALOT of money per month that could be saved for a house. The end result was we settled on a one owner used car, paid 7500 for it, got 8500 for my truck. Financially our loan was the same number of months (24 remained at the time) with the same payment (about 450). We got a nice car that is very enjoyable at a highly affordable price for us.

What I am trying to illustrate here is that throughout my experience of losing money consistently year over year and Iearned to moderate my spending, limit financing, and don't over buy while still enjoying what I do buy. I am also renting. I suspect that many millenials have had experiences similar to mine and are much more choosey about their spending and have given banks the finger while telling them to shove their loans for everything up their backside.
